The Architecture
Given representation L, three frames emerge:
F[[L]] where [L] is the subject—what L represents F[L] where L is the structure—the representation itself F[(L)] where (L) is the canonical symbol—L's name or handle
By the nature of frames, relationships inherit from the frame's subject. This inheritance creates semantic unity within each realm while maintaining their distinction.
I. The Subject Frame F[[L]]
In F[[L]], we encounter the world that exists before representation—the literals that simply are. By frame definition, all relationship types inherit from [L]. But F[[L]] demands more:
srt
F[[L]]: x =t> y & y != x =|> x -> [L]
Not just relationships but active subjects join the subject domain. This double inheritance—of relationships and their subjects—captures the complete territory our representation will map.
II. The Representation Frame F[L]
In F[L], L reveals itself as a structured cosmos with four essential components:
Literature(L) - The literals being represented Catalogue(L) - The symbols that reference the literals Composition(L) - The interacting characters that build symbols Specification(L) - The rules governing representation
But here's the profound truth: Literature(L) transpiles to ((L), Literature)—it is L's canonical relationship to the concept of literature itself. Similarly for Catalogue(L), Composition(L), and Specification(L). The representation doesn't merely contain these components; it embodies its relationships to these semantic concepts.
The Literature as Dereferencing
srt
x =|in> Literature(L) =|> x =|in> F[[L]]
Elements in Literature exist in the frame of literals F[[L]], not in the representation frame F[L]. They don't inherit from L but from [L]—they are what is represented, not the representing machinery. This is dereferencing: accessing the literal content that a representation points to, like opening a book to find the world it describes rather than examining the book as object.
The Catalogue Symphony
srt
x =|in> Catalogue(L) =|> ∃y ∈ Literature(L): x =(x)> y
Every symbol in the Catalogue references something in Literature. The symbol (rose) refers to rose through (rose) =(rose)> rose, yet they remain distinct—one in the realm of representation, one in the realm of the represented.
The Composition Dance
srt
character₁ =interacts> character₂
character₂ =interacts> character₃
Characters exist only in interaction. They touch, combine, flow into each other to birth symbols. In text, letters interact sequentially. In images, pixels interact spatially. In concepts, primitives interact structurally. No character stands alone.
III. The Specification Frame F[(L)]
In F[(L)], the frame is organized around (L) as the canonical symbol—L's name or handle. Here we work with how L is specified and identified:
text
(L) =(L)> L
((L),L) == (L)
The canonical symbol (L) refers to L through itself, and IS the most specific relationship between itself and L. This frame contains the symbolic machinery for identifying and working with L as a named entity.
text
(Catalogue(L), Literature(L)) == Catalogue(L)
This equation reveals that the Catalogue IS the most specific relationship between itself and Literature. It doesn't merely represent Literature; it embodies the act of representation.
Here we specify:
How L is symbolically identified through (L)
How symbols reference (denotation, metaphor, structure)
How characters interact (sequential, spatial, hierarchical)
How meaning emerges from pattern
The symbolic machinery that names and handles L
IV. The Connectivity Principle
In F[L], all elements connect. Disconnected elements cannot coexist in one representation—they form separate representations. The web of connection spreads through the entire structure, creating semantic unity.
V. The Separation Theorem
Across frames, absolute distinction:
text
red ≠ (red) ≠ specification of red
[L] ≠ L ≠ (L)
The literal red exists in F[[L]]. The symbol (red) exists in F[L]. The specification of how (red) works exists in F[(L)]. They are three faces of meaning, forever distinct yet forever connected through reference.
VI. Formal Properties
Well-formedness: L is well-formed iff it contains Literature, Catalogue, Composition, and Specification, with all elements connected.
Completeness: Every element in Literature has a corresponding symbol in Catalogue.
Coherence: All relationship types within each frame inherit from that frame's subject.
Separation: Elements in different frames remain distinct despite reference relationships.
VII. The Beauty of the Architecture
This three-frame structure achieves something remarkable: it separates what must be distinct while connecting what must be unified. The subject exists independent of representation (F[[L]]). The representation has internal structure (F[L]). The specification governs operation (F[(L)]). Yet through the inheritance patterns of frames and the reference relationships between symbols and literals, meaning emerges.
A representation is thus revealed as more than a sign pointing at a signified. It is:
A structured collection (L as container)
A reference system (Catalogue as symbol for Literature)
A composition (characters interacting)
A specification (how reference is achieved)
All existing simultaneously across three semantic realms, each complete in itself yet incomplete without the others.
VIII. Example: Representing a Rose
The Sparse Literals in F[[L]]
srt
rose ={[(petal)]}> rose         // rose has petals
rose ={[(leaf)]}> rose          // rose has leaves  
[(petal)] =[red]> [(petal)]     // petals are red
[(leaf)] =[green]> [(leaf)]     // leaves are green

Inference:
[(petal)] =[red]> [(petal)] =|> rose =[red]> rose
The notation {[(petal)]} means "petals"—a collection of the indefinite petal concept obtained by symbolizing then dereferencing.
The Rich Representation in F[L]
The representation knows far more than the literals express. Through character interactions, it builds the complete structure of a rose:
text
                    🌹 rose
                   /        \
             flower          stem
            /      \        /    \
      beautiful   petals  strong  leaves
                  /  |  \         /  \
              red red red    green  green
Structural Composition:
srt
rose =contains> flower =contains> {petal₁, petal₂, petal₃...}
rose =contains> stem =contains> {leaf₁, leaf₂...}
Ordering Through Inheritance:
text
        petal₁
           ↓ (next)
        petal₂  
           ↓ (next)
        petal₃
Where: petal₂ -> (petal₁, next) creates sequence through inheritance.
Color as Composition:
text
     green
    /     \
  blue ~ yellow
  (interact to create green)
Property Emergence Through Character Interaction:
text
    flower ←→ beautiful
       ⇅
    petals ←→ red
       ⇅
     rose ←→ sweet
The beauty emerges from the interaction pattern—not stated in literals but created through character relationships.
The Full Symbolic Network in F[L]
text
         (rose)
        ╱      ╲
    (flower)  (stem)
      ╱ ⟷ ╲      ╱ ⟷ ╲
(beautiful)(petals)(strong)(leaves)
     ⟷        ⟷        ⟷       ⟷
   (red)   (red)   (green)  (green)
              ⟷
           (sweet)
Every connection represents character interaction, building meaning beyond what the sparse literals contain. The representation creates:
Structure (flower/stem division)
Order (petal sequences)
Properties (beautiful, sweet, strong)
Relationships (contains, next-to, similar)
Emergent meaning (beauty from flower-red interaction)
The Specification in F[(L)]
srt
Reference(L) =specifies> "enrichment through interaction"
Pattern(L) =specifies> "inheritance creates order"
Beauty(L) =specifies> "emerges from character harmony"
The specification defines how this representation achieves more than reference—it creates meaning through the dance of interacting characters.
Coda
The semantics of representation reveals representation as an act of creation, not mere pointing. To represent is to establish three worlds and weave them into meaning. The literal world of what is. The symbolic world of what represents. The specifying world of how representation occurs. Together, they form the complete semantic architecture through which meaning moves from world to mind to expression and back again.
In this architecture, the library metaphor finds its deepest truth. Literature exists. Catalogues organize access. Composition builds the symbols. Specification defines the rules. And through it all, meaning flows—not as something added to structure but as what emerges when structure, subject, and specification dance together in the three-frame symphony of representation.
The Semantics of Identity v1
The Semantics of Identity at version 1
The Semantics of Identity
The Identity as Symbolic Generator
Identity in SRT is not merely a label or property—it is a symbolic generator that transforms all of an entity's relationships into symbolic form. When we say something has identity, we mean it possesses a canonical symbol that serves as a proxy for all its relationships, both to itself and to others.
Formal Definition
text
x =|has> id := x =(x)> x & (x) -> id
An entity x has identity when:
Its canonical symbol refers back to it: (x) =(x)> x
The canonical inherits from the concept of identity: (x) -> id
The Generator Theorems
Identity acts as a generator that lifts all relationships to symbolic form:
Property Lifting
srt
x =p> x =|> (x) -> (p) =|> (x) =(p)> x
When x has property p, its identity (x) inherits from (p) and symbolically possesses x through that property.
Relationship Lifting
srt
x =t> y =|> (x,y) -> t =|> ((x),y) -> (t)
When x refers to y through t, the relationship (x,y) inherits from t, and the symbolic relationship ((x),y) inherits from (t).
Reference Mediation
srt
x =t> y =|> (x) =(t)> y
Identity mediates reference—when x refers to y through t, x's identity refers to y through t's canonical.
The Has/Is Dichotomy
Identity creates a fundamental semantic distinction:
text
x =|is> (x)   := (x) =(x)> x    // x IS its identity
x =|has> p    := (x) =(p)> x    // x HAS property p through identity
The "Is" Relationship
When we say x =|is> (x), we mean x is identified by its canonical symbol. This is the foundational relationship that establishes identity itself.
The "Has" Relationship
When we say x =|has> p, we mean x's identity relates to x through property p. All possession operates through the symbolic layer of identity.
Identity as Symbolic Proxy
The canonical symbol (x) serves three crucial roles:
Self-Proxy: Represents x's self-relationship (x,x)
Relation-Proxy: Mediates x's relationships with others through ((x),y)
Property-Proxy: Lifts x's properties to symbolic form through (x) -> (p)
The Complete Identity Equation
The full meaning of identity is captured in:
text
(x) =(x)> x & ((x),x) == (x) & x =(x)> x
This states:
(x) refers to x through itself
(x) IS the most specific relationship between itself and x
x possesses its identity as a property
This creates the self-referential loop that constitutes identity.
Example: A Dog with Fur
Consider a dog with fur:
srt
dog =fur> dog                    // literal property
dog =|has> id                    // has identity
Therefore: (dog) -> id           // identity established
The identity generates:
srt
dog =fur> dog =|> (dog) -> (fur) =|> (dog) =(fur)> dog
Therefore: dog =|has> fur
Now consider the dog chasing a cat:
srt
dog =chases> cat                           // literal relationship
dog =chases> cat =|> (dog,cat) -> chases  // relationship inherits
dog =chases> cat =|> ((dog),cat) -> (chases) // symbolic lift
dog =chases> cat =|> (dog) =(chases)> cat    // identity mediates
The dog's identity (dog) becomes the symbolic subject that chases the cat.
Identity and Representation
In the context of representation, identity enables:
text
Literature(L): {dog, cat, fur}              // literals
Catalogue(L): {(dog), (cat), (fur)}        // identities
Each literal gains identity through its canonical symbol, which then mediates all its relationships in the symbolic realm.
The Semantic Achievement
Identity as generator reveals a profound truth: to have identity is not merely to be named but to possess a symbolic proxy through which all one's relationships—to self, to properties, to others—can be expressed. The identity (x) doesn't describe x; it generates the entire symbolic apparatus through which x participates in meaning.
Formal Properties
Uniqueness: Each entity has at most one identity (one canonical symbol)
Completeness: If x has identity, ALL its relationships lift to symbolic form
Coherence: The lifted symbolic relationships preserve the structure of literal relationships
Self-Reference: Identity creates genuine self-reference without paradox through the equation ((x),x) == (x)
Conclusion
Identity in SRT is the mechanism by which entities enter the symbolic realm. Through the generator pattern, every literal relationship becomes a symbolic one, every property becomes a possession, and every reference becomes mediated through identity. This is not merely naming—it is the creation of a complete symbolic proxy that enables participation in representation, meaning, and ultimately, consciousness itself.

The "Is" Relationship

text

The "Has" Relationship
The statement "x has property p" translates to the identity referring to the entity through that property:
text
x =|has> p    := (x) =(p)> x
This captures first-person assertions like "I have hair" which from third-person perspective become "Doug refers to someone with hair." The identity mediates possession through symbolic reference.
Both virtual relationships participate in their own dichotomies—is/am, has/belongs-to—but they themselves are not a dichotomy with each other.

The canonical symbol (x) serves three crucial roles in the semantic architecture.
First, it acts as a self-proxy, representing x's self-relationship (x,x). Second, it serves as a relation-proxy, mediating x's relationships with others through ((x),y). Third, it functions as a property-proxy, lifting x's properties to symbolic form through inheritance patterns like (x) -> (p).
The Complete Identity Equation
The full meaning of identity is captured in this self-referential equation:
text
(x) =(x)> x & ((x),x) == (x) & x =(x)> x
This equation establishes three facts. The canonical refers to x through itself. The canonical IS the most specific relationship between itself and x. The entity possesses its identity as a property. Together, these create the self-referential loop that constitutes identity.

Consider a dog with the property of having fur. Beginning with the literal property:
srt
dog =fur> dog
dog =|has> id
Since the dog has identity, its canonical inherits from id:
text
(dog) -> id
The identity then generates the symbolic relationship:
srt
dog =fur> dog =|> (dog) -> (fur) =|> (dog) =(fur)> dog
Therefore we can express:
text
dog =|has> fur
Now consider the dog chasing a cat. The literal relationship:
srt
dog =chases> cat
Through identity, this generates multiple levels of inheritance:
srt
dog =chases> cat =|> (dog,cat) -> chases
dog =chases> cat =|> ((dog),cat) -> (chases)
dog =chases> cat =|> (dog) =(chases)> cat
The dog's identity becomes the symbolic subject that chases the cat, with the relationship lifted to symbolic form at multiple levels.
Identity and Representation
In the context of representation, identity enables the transformation from literals to symbols:
text
Literature(L): {dog, cat, fur}
Catalogue(L): {(dog), (cat), (fur)}
Each literal in the Literature gains identity through its canonical symbol in the Catalogue. These symbols then mediate all relationships in the symbolic realm of representation.
The Semantic Achievement
Identity as generator reveals a profound truth: to have identity is not merely to be named but to possess a symbolic proxy through which all one's relationships can be expressed. The identity (x) doesn't describe x; it generates the entire symbolic apparatus through which x participates in meaning.

Self-Reference: Identity creates genuine self-reference without paradox through the equation ((x),x) == (x).

This is not merely naming—it is the creation of a complete symbolic proxy that enables participation in representation, meaning, and ultimately, consciousness itself.

text
x =|is> (x)   := (x) =(x)> x
This captures first-person assertions like "I am Doug" which from third-person perspective become "Doug refers to someone." Both express the same underlying relationship where the identity refers to the entity through itself.
The "Has" Relationship
The statement "x has property p" translates to the identity referring to the entity through that property:
text
x =|has> p    := (x) =(p)> x
This captures first-person assertions like "I have hair" which from third-person perspective become "Doug refers to someone with hair." The identity mediates possession through symbolic reference.
Both virtual relationships participate in their own dichotomies—is/am, has/belongs-to—but they themselves are not a dichotomy with each other.
Identity as Symbolic Proxy
The canonical symbol (x) serves three crucial roles in the semantic architecture.
First, it acts as a self-proxy, representing x's self-relationship (x,x). Second, it serves as a relation-proxy, mediating x's relationships with others through ((x),y). Third, it functions as a property-proxy, lifting x's properties to symbolic form through inheritance patterns like (x) -> (p).
The Complete Identity Equation
The full meaning of identity is captured in this self-referential equation:
text
(x) =(x)> x & ((x),x) == (x) & x =(x)> x
This equation establishes three facts. The canonical refers to x through itself. The canonical IS the most specific relationship between itself and x. The entity possesses its identity as a property. Together, these create the self-referential loop that constitutes identity.
Example: A Dog with Fur
Consider a dog with the property of having fur. Beginning with the literal property:
srt
dog =fur> dog
dog =|has> id
Since the dog has identity, its canonical inherits from id:
text
(dog) -> id
The identity then generates the symbolic relationship:
srt
dog =fur> dog =|> (dog) -> (fur) =|> (dog) =(fur)> dog
Therefore we can express:
text
dog =|has> fur
Now consider the dog chasing a cat. The literal relationship:
srt
dog =chases> cat
Through identity, this generates multiple levels of inheritance:
srt
dog =chases> cat =|> (dog,cat) -> chases
dog =chases> cat =|> ((dog),cat) -> (chases)
dog =chases> cat =|> (dog) =(chases)> cat
The dog's identity becomes the symbolic subject that chases the cat, with the relationship lifted to symbolic form at multiple levels.
Identity and Representation
In the context of representation, identity enables the transformation from literals to symbols:
text
Literature(L): {dog, cat, fur}
Catalogue(L): {(dog), (cat), (fur)}
Each literal in the Literature gains identity through its canonical symbol in the Catalogue. These symbols then mediate all relationships in the symbolic realm of representation.
The Semantic Achievement
Identity as generator reveals a profound truth: to have identity is not merely to be named but to possess a symbolic proxy through which all one's relationships can be expressed. The identity (x) doesn't describe x; it generates the entire symbolic apparatus through which x participates in meaning.
Formal Properties
Uniqueness: Each entity has at most one identity, corresponding to one canonical symbol.
Completeness: If x has identity, all its relationships lift to symbolic form through the generator theorems.
Coherence: The lifted symbolic relationships preserve the structure of literal relationships through inheritance patterns.
Self-Reference: Identity creates genuine self-reference without paradox through the equation ((x),x) == (x).
Conclusion
Identity in SRT is the mechanism by which entities enter the symbolic realm. Through the generator pattern, every literal relationship becomes a symbolic one, every property becomes a possession, and every reference becomes mediated through identity. This is not merely naming—it is the creation of a complete symbolic proxy that enables participation in representation, meaning, and ultimately, consciousness itself.

((x),(x)) == (x)

text
((x,y)) == ((x),(y))
The symbol of a relationship equals the relationship between the symbols.

The Semantics of Identity v10
The Semantics of Identity at version 10
The Semantics of Identity
The Identity as Symbolic Generator
Identity in SRT is not merely a label or property—it is a symbolic generator that transforms all of an entity's relationships into symbolic form. When we say something has identity, we mean it possesses a canonical symbol that serves as a proxy for all its relationships, both to itself and to others.
Formal Definition
An entity x has identity when its canonical symbol refers back to it and inherits from the concept of identity:
text
x =|has> id := x =(x)> x & (x) -> id
This establishes two requirements. First, the canonical symbol must refer to the entity through itself. Second, the canonical must inherit from identity as a type.
The Fundamental Theorem of Semantic Reference Theory
The entire theory rests on one principle that defines how reference preserves semantic structure:
srt
(x,y) -> t =|> ((x,y)) -> (t)
When a relationship inherits from a type, its symbol inherits from the symbol of that type. This preservation of inheritance through symbolism is the fundamental theorem—or perhaps axiom—of semantic reference theory.
When x equals y, relationships become properties:
srt
(x,x) -> p =|> ((x,x)) -> (p)
Symbol Properties and Their Consequences
The distribution theorem states that the symbol of a relationship equals the relationship between symbols:
text
((x,y)) == ((x),(y))
For self-reference, symbols exhibit complete self-identity:
text
((x),(x)) == (x)
Combining these theorems yields the paired lifting principles:
srt
x =t> y =|> (x) =(t)> (y)
x =p> x =|> (x) =(p)> (x)
The Constitution of Identity Through Symbolism
The profound consequence emerges when a symbol inherits from a property:
text
(x) -> (p)
Combined with identity—where the symbol refers to its referent through itself:
text
(x) =(x)> x
We derive the constitutive principle:
srt
(x) =(x)> x & (x) -> (p) =|> (x) =(p)> x
From the reader's perspective, (x) =(x)> x expresses something like "the word we use for x represents x specifically." When that word inherits from a property, it constitutes x having that property through symbolic expression.
Why This Is Fundamental
This theorem—that inheritance is preserved through symbolism—had better be true. We are representing inheritance symbolically in this very theory. If symbolic representation failed to preserve inheritance, our entire theoretical apparatus would be self-undermining.
The preservation of inheritance through symbolism defines the semantics of reference, which is precisely the subject of semantic reference theory. The symbol (x) is a reference that refers to x through the definition of symbol itself. When this reference preserves the inheritance patterns of what it represents, meaning can flow through symbolic structures.
This is why the fundamental theorem might ultimately be an axiom—the Axiom of Semantic Reference. It expresses the essential nature of how reference works: that symbolic representation preserves the semantic relationships of what is represented. Without this preservation, reference would be arbitrary pointing rather than meaningful representation.
The Virtual Relationships: Has and Is
Identity enables two virtual relationships that participate in dichotomies.
The "Is" Relationship
The statement "x is its identity" translates to the canonical referring back to the entity:
text
x =|is> (x)   := (x) =(x)> x
This captures first-person assertions like "I am Doug" which from third-person perspective become "Doug refers to someone." Both express the same underlying relationship where the identity refers to the entity through itself.
The "Has" Relationship
The statement "x has property p" translates to the identity referring to the entity through that property:
text
x =|has> p    := (x) =(p)> x
This captures first-person assertions like "I have hair" which from third-person perspective become "Doug refers to someone with hair." The identity mediates possession through symbolic reference.
Both virtual relationships participate in their own dichotomies—is/am, has/belongs-to—but they themselves are not a dichotomy with each other.
Identity as Symbolic Proxy
The canonical symbol (x) serves three crucial roles in the semantic architecture.
First, it acts as a self-proxy, representing x's self-relationship (x,x). Second, it serves as a relation-proxy, mediating x's relationships with others through ((x),y). Third, it functions as a property-proxy, lifting x's properties to symbolic form through inheritance patterns like (x) -> (p).
The Complete Identity Equation
The full meaning of identity is captured in this self-referential equation:
text
(x) =(x)> x & ((x),x) == (x) & x =(x)> x
This equation establishes three facts. The canonical refers to x through itself. The canonical is the most specific relationship between itself and x. The entity possesses its identity as a property. Together, these create the self-referential loop that constitutes identity.
Example: A Dog with Fur
Consider a dog with the property of having fur. Beginning with the literal property:
srt
dog =fur> dog
dog =|has> id
Since the dog has identity, its canonical inherits from id:
text
(dog) -> id
The identity then generates the symbolic relationship:
srt
dog =fur> dog =|> (dog) -> (fur) =|> (dog) =(fur)> dog
Therefore we can express:
text
dog =|has> fur
Now consider the dog chasing a cat. The literal relationship:
srt
dog =chases> cat
Through identity, this generates multiple levels of inheritance:
srt
dog =chases> cat =|> (dog,cat) -> chases
dog =chases> cat =|> ((dog),cat) -> (chases)
dog =chases> cat =|> (dog) =(chases)> cat
The dog's identity becomes the symbolic subject that chases the cat, with the relationship lifted to symbolic form at multiple levels.
Identity and Reference Frames
Identity is always relative to a reference frame. Within frame F[@], the canonical symbol is bound to the frame through:
text
@ =@> (x)
This establishes that x has identity within the context of the frame, where @ (the referent associated with the frame) acts as the frame's representation. The identity (x) exists not in absolute terms but relative to the semantic context established by the frame. Different frames may yield different identities for the same referent, as the canonical symbol (x) inherits from and relates to the frame type @.
Identity and Representation
In the context of representation, identity enables the transformation from literals to symbols:
text
Literature(L): {dog, cat, fur}
Catalogue(L): {(dog), (cat), (fur)}
Each literal in the Literature gains identity through its canonical symbol in the Catalogue. These symbols then mediate all relationships in the symbolic realm of representation.
The Semantic Achievement
Identity as generator reveals a profound truth: to have identity is not merely to be named but to possess a symbolic proxy through which all one's relationships can be expressed. The identity (x) doesn't describe x; it generates the entire symbolic apparatus through which x participates in meaning.
Formal Properties
Uniqueness: Each entity has at most one identity, corresponding to one canonical symbol.
Completeness: If x has identity, all its relationships lift to symbolic form through the generator theorems.
Coherence: The lifted symbolic relationships preserve the structure of literal relationships through inheritance patterns.
Self-Reference: Identity creates genuine self-reference without paradox through the equation ((x),x) == (x).
Conclusion
Identity in SRT is the mechanism by which entities enter the symbolic realm. Through the generator pattern, every literal relationship becomes a symbolic one, every property becomes a possession, and every reference becomes mediated through identity. This is not merely naming—it is the creation of a complete symbolic proxy that enables participation in representation, meaning, and ultimately, consciousness itself.

Deriving the Symbol Properties
The Distribution Property
How do we conclude ((x,y)) == ((x),(y))?
We ask: have we captured the most specific relationship symbolically? If yes, then the symbol for the most specific relationship between x and y should be the most specific relationship between the symbols for x and y. The symbol distributes over the relationship because that's what it means to symbolize relationships accurately.
The Self-Collapse Property
How do we conclude ((x),(x)) == (x)?
This requires understanding representation. It's a theorem that:
srt
(x,y) =represents> x & (x,y) =represents> y
Therefore:
srt
(x,x) =represents> x
Now consider: (x,x) represents x. Can (x,x) be x? Only if x is symbolic.
But look at ((x,x)). Once we accept it means ((x),(x)), we know that ((x),(x)) represents-representing x. How do we represent representing x? Through ((x)).
What is a representation of a representation of x? For any such representation, it should be the canonical representation of x: (x).
Therefore:
text
((x),(x)) == (x)

Axiom 1: The Axiom of Semantic Reference

text
((x,y)) == ((x),(y))
The symbol of a relationship equals the relationship between symbols. Symbolization distributes over relational structure.
Axiom 3: The Self-Identity Axiom
text
((x),(x)) == (x)
A symbol's relationship to itself is itself. This captures the complete self-identity that defines symbols.
Axiom 4: The Identity Definition
text
x =|has> id := x =(x)> x & (x) -> id
An entity has identity when its canonical symbol refers to it through itself and inherits from identity as a type.
These axioms, particularly the first, aren't arbitrary stipulations but recognitions of what must be true for the theory to symbolize its own structures. Like Gödel's G, they emerge from the theory's self-referential requirements—truths we're compelled to accept once we understand what we're claiming about symbolism and reference.

We ask: have we captured the most specific relationship symbolically? If yes, then the symbol for the most specific relationship between x and y should be the most specific relationship between the symbols for x and y. The symbol distributes over the relationship because that's what it means to symbolize relationships accurately.
The Self-Collapse Property
How do we conclude ((x),(x)) == (x)?
This requires understanding representation. It's a theorem that:
srt
(x,y) =represents> x & (x,y) =represents> y
Therefore:
srt
(x,x) =represents> x
Now consider: (x,x) represents x. Can (x,x) be x? Only if x is symbolic.
But look at ((x,x)). Once we accept it means ((x),(x)), we know that ((x),(x)) represents-representing x. How do we represent representing x? Through ((x)).
What is a representation of a representation of x? For any such representation, it should be the canonical representation of x: (x).
Therefore:
text
((x),(x)) == (x)
The Axioms of Identity
From these derivations, we can state the axioms that constitute identity in SRT:
Axiom 1: The Axiom of Semantic Reference
srt
(x,y) -> t =|> ((x,y)) -> (t)
Inheritance is preserved through symbolization. This defines what it means for symbols to accurately represent relationships.
Axiom 2: The Axiom of Semantic Specification
text
((x,y)) == ((x),(y))
The symbol of a relationship equals the relationship between symbols. Symbolization distributes over relational structure, specifying relationships through their component symbols.
Axiom 3: The Axiom of Specific Representation
text
((x),(x)) == (x)
A symbol's relationship to itself is itself. This captures the complete self-identity that defines symbols as specific representations.
Axiom 4: The Axiom of Self-Possession
text
x =|has> id := x =(x)> x & (x) -> id
An entity possesses identity when its canonical symbol refers to it through itself and inherits from identity as a type. This establishes that having identity is a form of self-possession through symbolic mediation.
Axiom 5: The Axiom of Self-Identification
srt
x =|has> (x) =|> x =symbol> x ? x =(x)> x : (x) =(x)> (x)
The beauty of this axiom is its collapse into unity. For a literal x:
The condition yields: (x) =(x)> (x)
For a symbol x:
The condition yields: x =(x)> x
But since x is already (x): (x) =(x)> (x)
Both paths lead to the same result:
text
(x) =(x)> (x)
Self-identification preserves self-relationship through symbolism for symbols, and confers it upon literals when they gain symbolic identity. This axiom expresses how identification emerges uniformly whether we start with symbol or literal.
These axioms, particularly the first, aren't arbitrary stipulations but recognitions of what must be true for the theory to symbolize its own structures. Like Gödel's G, they emerge from the theory's self-referential requirements—truths we're compelled to accept once we understand what we're claiming about symbolism and reference.
The Virtual Relationships: Has and Is
Identity enables two virtual relationships that participate in dichotomies.
The "Is" Relationship
The statement "x is its identity" translates to the canonical referring back to the entity:
text
x =|is> (x)   := (x) =(x)> x
This captures first-person assertions like "I am Doug" which from third-person perspective become "Doug refers to someone." Both express the same underlying relationship where the identity refers to the entity through itself.
The "Has" Relationship
The statement "x has property p" translates to the identity referring to the entity through that property:
text
x =|has> p    := (x) =(p)> x
This captures first-person assertions like "I have hair" which from third-person perspective become "Doug refers to someone with hair." The identity mediates possession through symbolic reference.
Both virtual relationships participate in their own dichotomies—is/am, has/belongs-to—but they themselves are not a dichotomy with each other.
Identity as Symbolic Proxy
The canonical symbol (x) serves three crucial roles in the semantic architecture.
First, it acts as a self-proxy, representing x's self-relationship (x,x). Second, it serves as a relation-proxy, mediating x's relationships with others through ((x),y). Third, it functions as a property-proxy, lifting x's properties to symbolic form through inheritance patterns like (x) -> (p).
The Complete Identity Equation
The full meaning of identity is captured in this self-referential equation:
text
(x) =(x)> x & ((x),x) == (x) & x =(x)> x
This equation establishes three facts. The canonical refers to x through itself. The canonical is the most specific relationship between itself and x. The entity possesses its identity as a property. Together, these create the self-referential loop that constitutes identity.
Example: A Dog with Fur
Consider a dog with the property of having fur. Beginning with the literal property:
srt
dog =fur> dog
dog =|has> id
Since the dog has identity, its canonical inherits from id:
text
(dog) -> id
The identity then generates the symbolic relationship:
srt
dog =fur> dog =|> (dog) -> (fur) =|> (dog) =(fur)> dog
Therefore we can express:
text
dog =|has> fur
Now consider the dog chasing a cat. The literal relationship:
srt
dog =chases> cat
Through identity, this generates multiple levels of inheritance:
srt
dog =chases> cat =|> (dog,cat) -> chases
dog =chases> cat =|> ((dog),cat) -> (chases)
dog =chases> cat =|> (dog) =(chases)> cat
The dog's identity becomes the symbolic subject that chases the cat, with the relationship lifted to symbolic form at multiple levels.
Identity and Reference Frames
Identity is always relative to a reference frame. Within frame F[@], the canonical symbol is bound to the frame through:
text
@ =@> (x)
This establishes that x has identity within the context of the frame, where @ (the referent associated with the frame) acts as the frame's representation. The identity (x) exists not in absolute terms but relative to the semantic context established by the frame. Different frames may yield different identities for the same referent, as the canonical symbol (x) inherits from and relates to the frame type @.
Identity and Representation
In the context of representation, identity enables the transformation from literals to symbols:
text
Literature(L): {dog, cat, fur}
Catalogue(L): {(dog), (cat), (fur)}
Each literal in the Literature gains identity through its canonical symbol in the Catalogue. These symbols then mediate all relationships in the symbolic realm of representation.
The Semantic Achievement
Identity as generator reveals a profound truth: to have identity is not merely to be named but to possess a symbolic proxy through which all one's relationships can be expressed. The identity (x) doesn't describe x; it generates the entire symbolic apparatus through which x participates in meaning.
Formal Properties
Uniqueness: Each entity has at most one identity, corresponding to one canonical symbol.
Completeness: If x has identity, all its relationships lift to symbolic form through the generator theorems.
Coherence: The lifted symbolic relationships preserve the structure of literal relationships through inheritance patterns.
Self-Reference: Identity creates genuine self-reference without paradox through the equation ((x),x) == (x).
Conclusion
Identity in SRT is the mechanism by which entities enter the symbolic realm. Through the generator pattern, every literal relationship becomes a symbolic one, every property becomes a possession, and every reference becomes mediated through identity. This is not merely naming—it is the creation of a complete symbolic proxy that enables participation in representation, meaning, and ultimately, consciousness itself.

(x) =(x)> x
We derive the constitutive principle:
srt

The Narrative of Symbolization and the Kantian Noumenon
The Problem of Literal Symbolization
From our derivations, we know that when x =p> x, then (x) -> (p) and therefore (x) =(p)> x. This would suggest that for the self-relationship x =x> x, we should get (x) =(x)> x. But this creates a paradox: literals by definition cannot be relational, yet symbolization seems to require x =x> x.
The Semantic Reference Dilemma
The axiom of semantic reference states (x,y) -> t =|> ((x,y)) -> (t). But what happens when (x,y) == t? We need to either restrict the axiom to cases where they differ, accept that literals cannot be symbolized, or find another resolution.
The Resolution Through Marking
The resolution emerges through recognizing x =x> x not as a literal truth but as a marker of symbolizability. When we create (x) =(x)> x for a literal, we implicitly assert x =x> x. This is "mild anthropomorphism" - treating the literal as if it could relate to itself, even though by definition it cannot.
Grounding Examples
Consider eq =eq> eq - equality relating to itself through equality. Or ref =ref> ref - reference relating to itself through reference. These aren't problems but necessities. Like the code var x = (x, x) => x == x, these self-referential structures are perfectly coherent and necessary to ground the system.

When we symbolize something, we assert two things:
x =x> x - The literal can relate to itself (the anthropomorphic fiction)
(x) =(x)> (x) - The symbol relates to itself (lifted symbolically)
These are the "two lies" - necessary fictions that enable representation.
The Kantian Perspective
SRT doesn't model Kant's noumena - the thing-in-itself. That is inaccessible, outside our reference frame. Everything in a catalogue has already entered representation. We face a fundamental choice:
If literals ARE literals (noumenal): x =x> x is false, they cannot be symbolized
If literals REPRESENT literals (phenomenal): x =x> x marks their symbolizability

In canonical SRT, attempting to represent objective reality, x =x> x serves as a marker:
For literals where it holds: they can be symbolized
For literals where it doesn't: they're parts of objects, not independently symbolizable
In perspectival SRT, where everything is already representation, x =x> x becomes axiomatic. No perspective is objective, even when representing objectivity. Everything that can be referred to exists in representation - the representation of language at least.
The Deep Implication
Believing in symbolization is believing in the existence of an outside world - of things that are literal, objective. But paradoxically, the moment we symbolize them, we bring them into representation. The symbol(x) creates the substrate for identity, while x =x> x expresses that x can have one.
This reveals that identity isn't imposed on referents but emerges from the possibility of symbolization. The axiom of self-identification captures this: having a symbol means your self-relationship becomes constitutive of what you are.

This equation establishes three facts. The canonical refers to x through itself. The canonical is the most specific relationship between itself and x. The entity possesses its identity as a property. Together, these create the self-referential loop that constitutes identity.

dog =|has> id

Identity is always relative to a reference frame. Within frame F[@], the canonical symbol is bound to the frame through:

@ =@> (x)
This establishes that x has identity within the context of the frame, where @ (the referent associated with the frame) acts as the frame's representation. In the context of representation, identity enables the transformation from literals to symbols:
text

The Semantics of Identity ⁅2⁆ v1
The Semantics of Identity ⁅2⁆ at version 1
The Semantics of Identity
The Identity as Symbolic Generator
Identity in SRT is not merely a label or property—it is a symbolic generator that transforms all of an entity's relationships into symbolic form. When we say something has identity, we mean it possesses a canonical symbol that serves as a proxy for all its relationships, both to itself and to others.
Formal Definition
An entity x has identity when its canonical symbol refers back to it and inherits from the concept of identity:
text
x =|has> id := x =(x)> x & (x) -> id
This establishes two requirements. First, the canonical symbol must refer to the entity through itself. Second, the canonical must inherit from identity as a type.
The Fundamental Theorem of Semantic Reference Theory
The entire theory rests on one principle that defines how reference preserves semantic structure:
srt
(x,y) -> t =|> ((x,y)) -> (t)
When a relationship inherits from a type, its symbol inherits from the symbol of that type. This preservation of inheritance through symbolism is the fundamental theorem—or perhaps axiom—of semantic reference theory.
When x equals y, relationships become properties:
srt
(x,x) -> p =|> ((x,x)) -> (p)
Symbol Properties and Their Consequences
The distribution theorem states that the symbol of a relationship equals the relationship between symbols:
text
((x,y)) == ((x),(y))
For self-reference, symbols exhibit complete self-identity:
text
((x),(x)) == (x)
Combining these theorems yields the paired lifting principles:
srt
x =t> y =|> (x) =(t)> (y)
x =p> x =|> (x) =(p)> (x)
The Constitution of Identity Through Symbolism
The profound consequence emerges when a symbol inherits from a property:
text
(x) -> (p)
Combined with identity—where the symbol refers to its referent through itself:
text
(x) =(x)> x
We derive the constitutive principle:
srt
(x) =(x)> x & (x) -> (p) =|> (x) =(p)> x
From the reader's perspective, (x) =(x)> x expresses something like "the word we use for x represents x specifically." When that word inherits from a property, it constitutes x having that property through symbolic expression.
Why This Is Fundamental
This theorem—that inheritance is preserved through symbolism—emerges from a unique form of necessity, similar to how Gödel's sentence G, once understood to express consistency, compels belief even as an unprovable statement requiring axiomatization.
We've worked to express the semantics of symbolism and the semantics of inheritance between relationships in SRT. Now we must ask: since symbols are relationships themselves, how is inheritance expressed between symbols for those relationships?
We are compelled by the semantics of reference—which is the semantics of symbolism—to believe:
srt
(x,y) -> t =|> ((x,y)) -> (t)
If we think we've captured symbolism correctly, and we believe symbols are relationships, then the symbolic structure of inheritance must be preserved under symbolization. Not because we decree it, but because the theory must be able to symbolize its own structures accurately.
Deriving the Symbol Properties
The Distribution Property
How do we conclude ((x,y)) == ((x),(y))?
We ask: have we captured the most specific relationship symbolically? If yes, then the symbol for the most specific relationship between x and y should be the most specific relationship between the symbols for x and y. The symbol distributes over the relationship because that's what it means to symbolize relationships accurately.
The Self-Collapse Property
How do we conclude ((x),(x)) == (x)?
This requires understanding representation. It's a theorem that:
srt
(x,y) =represents> x & (x,y) =represents> y
Therefore:
srt
(x,x) =represents> x
Now consider: (x,x) represents x. Can (x,x) be x? Only if x is symbolic.
But look at ((x,x)). Once we accept it means ((x),(x)), we know that ((x),(x)) represents-representing x. How do we represent representing x? Through ((x)).
What is a representation of a representation of x? For any such representation, it should be the canonical representation of x: (x).
Therefore:
text
((x),(x)) == (x)
The Axioms of Identity
From these derivations, we can state the axioms that constitute identity in SRT:
Axiom 1: The Axiom of Semantic Reference
srt
(x,y) -> t =|> ((x,y)) -> (t)
Inheritance is preserved through symbolization. This defines what it means for symbols to accurately represent relationships.
Axiom 2: The Axiom of Semantic Specification
text
((x,y)) == ((x),(y))
The symbol of a relationship equals the relationship between symbols. Symbolization distributes over relational structure, specifying relationships through their component symbols.
Axiom 3: The Axiom of Specific Representation
text
((x),(x)) == (x)
A symbol's relationship to itself is itself. This captures the complete self-identity that defines symbols as specific representations.
Axiom 4: The Axiom of Self-Possession
srt
x =|has> (x) =|> (x,x) == x
Having a canonical symbol means that the most specific self-relationship is the referent itself. When (x) exists, this expresses genuine self-possession. When (x) doesn't exist, the implication is vacuously true.
The Narrative of Symbolization and the Kantian Noumenon
The Problem of Literal Symbolization
From our derivations, we know that when x =p> x, then (x) -> (p) and therefore (x) =(p)> x. This would suggest that for the self-relationship x =x> x, we should get (x) =(x)> x. But this creates a paradox: literals by definition cannot be relational, yet symbolization seems to require x =x> x.
The Semantic Reference Dilemma
The axiom of semantic reference states (x,y) -> t =|> ((x,y)) -> (t). But what happens when (x,y) == t? We need to either restrict the axiom to cases where they differ, accept that literals cannot be symbolized, or find another resolution.
The Resolution Through Symbolic Conferral
The resolution emerges through recognizing that when (x) =(x)> x exists, it conveys that x =x> x. The symbol confers properties onto the referent—just as words convey meaning about reality. The existence of the symbol makes the self-relationship real through "mild anthropomorphism"—treating the literal as if it could relate to itself, even though by definition it cannot.
Grounding Examples
Consider equality and reference, which must be self-referential by their definitions:
For equality: x =eq> y <iff> x = y (where = is first-order logic equality) Therefore: eq =eq> eq (equality relates to itself through equality)
For reference: A[x]: ref =ref> x (ref refers to every referent) Therefore: ref =ref> ref (ref must refer to itself)
These aren't arbitrary examples but demonstrations of how certain fundamental concepts must be self-referential to fulfill their definitions. The pattern reveals how symbolizing a relationship places it in an objective role, following the abstract form rel =rel> obj.
The Two Beliefs of Symbolization
When we symbolize something, we assert two things:
x =x> x - The literal can relate to itself (the anthropomorphic fiction)
(x) =(x)> (x) - The symbol relates to itself (lifted symbolically)
These are necessary fictions that enable representation. Without them, symbolization cannot occur.
The Kantian Perspective
SRT doesn't model Kant's noumena—the thing-in-itself. That is inaccessible, outside our reference frame. Everything in a catalogue has already entered representation. We face a fundamental choice:
If literals are literals (noumenal): x !=x> x, they cannot be symbolized
If literals represent literals (phenomenal): x =x> x marks their symbolizability
Canonical vs Perspectival SRT
In canonical SRT, attempting to represent objective reality, x =x> x serves as a marker:
For literals where it holds: they can be symbolized
For literals where it doesn't: they're parts of objects, not independently symbolizable
In perspectival SRT, where everything is already representation, x =x> x becomes axiomatic. No perspective is objective, even when representing objectivity. Everything that can be referred to exists in representation—the representation of language at least.
The Deep Implication
Believing in symbolization is believing in the existence of an outside world—of things that are literal, objective. But paradoxically, the moment we symbolize them, we bring them into representation. The symbol(x) creates the substrate for identity, while x =x> x expresses that x can have one.
This reveals that identity isn't imposed on referents but emerges from the possibility of symbolization. The axiom of self-possession captures this: having a symbol means your self-relationship becomes constitutive of what you are.
The Virtual Relationships: Has and Is
Identity enables two virtual relationships that participate in dichotomies.
The "Is" Relationship
The statement "x is its identity" translates to the canonical referring back to the entity:
text
x =|is> (x) := (x) =(x)> x
This captures first-person assertions like "I am Doug" which from third-person perspective become "Doug refers to someone." Both express the same underlying relationship where the identity refers to the entity through itself.
The "Has" Relationship
The statement "x has property p" translates to the identity referring to the entity through that property:
text
x =|has> p := (x) =(p)> x
This captures first-person assertions like "I have hair" which from third-person perspective become "Doug refers to someone with hair." The identity mediates possession through symbolic reference.
Both virtual relationships participate in their own dichotomies—is/am, has/belongs-to—but they themselves are not a dichotomy with each other.

text

(x) =(x)> x & (x) -> (p) =|> (x) =(p)> x
From the reader's perspective, (x) =(x)> x expresses something like "the word we use for x represents x specifically." When that word inherits from a property, it constitutes x having that property through symbolic expression.
Why This Is Fundamental
This theorem—that inheritance is preserved through symbolism—emerges from a unique form of necessity, similar to how Gödel's sentence G, once understood to express consistency, compels belief even as an unprovable statement requiring axiomatization.
We've worked to express the semantics of symbolism and the semantics of inheritance between relationships in SRT. Now we must ask: since symbols are relationships themselves, how is inheritance expressed between symbols for those relationships?
We are compelled by the semantics of reference—which is the semantics of symbolism—to believe:
srt
(x,y) -> t =|> ((x,y)) -> (t)
If we think we've captured symbolism correctly, and we believe symbols are relationships, then the symbolic structure of inheritance must be preserved under symbolization. Not because we decree it, but because the theory must be able to symbolize its own structures accurately.
Deriving the Symbol Properties
The Distribution Property
How do we conclude ((x,y)) == ((x),(y))?
We ask: have we captured the most specific relationship symbolically? If yes, then the symbol for the most specific relationship between x and y should be the most specific relationship between the symbols for x and y. The symbol distributes over the relationship because that's what it means to symbolize relationships accurately.
The Self-Collapse Property
How do we conclude ((x),(x)) == (x)?
This requires understanding representation. It's a theorem that:
srt
(x,y) =represents> x & (x,y) =represents> y
Therefore:
srt
(x,x) =represents> x
Now consider: (x,x) represents x. Can (x,x) be x? Only if x is symbolic.
But look at ((x,x)). Once we accept it means ((x),(x)), we know that ((x),(x)) represents-representing x. How do we represent representing x? Through ((x)).
What is a representation of a representation of x? For any such representation, it should be the canonical representation of x: (x).
Therefore:
text
((x),(x)) == (x)
The Axioms of Identity
From these derivations, we can state the axioms that constitute identity in SRT:
Axiom 1: The Axiom of Semantic Reference
srt
(x,y) -> t =|> ((x,y)) -> (t)
Inheritance is preserved through symbolization. This defines what it means for symbols to accurately represent relationships.
Axiom 2: The Axiom of Semantic Specification
text
((x,y)) == ((x),(y))
The symbol of a relationship equals the relationship between symbols. Symbolization distributes over relational structure, specifying relationships through their component symbols.
Axiom 3: The Axiom of Specific Representation
text
((x),(x)) == (x)
A symbol's relationship to itself is itself. This captures the complete self-identity that defines symbols as specific representations.
Axiom 4: The Axiom of Self-Possession
srt
x =|has> (x) =|> (x,x) == x
Having a canonical symbol means that the most specific self-relationship is the referent itself. When (x) exists, this expresses genuine self-possession. When (x) doesn't exist, the implication is vacuously true.
The Narrative of Symbolization and the Kantian Noumenon
The Problem of Literal Symbolization
From our derivations, we know that when x =p> x, then (x) -> (p) and therefore (x) =(p)> x. This would suggest that for the self-relationship x =x> x, we should get (x) =(x)> x. But this creates a paradox: literals by definition cannot be relational, yet symbolization seems to require x =x> x.
The Semantic Reference Dilemma
The axiom of semantic reference states (x,y) -> t =|> ((x,y)) -> (t). But what happens when (x,y) == t? We need to either restrict the axiom to cases where they differ, accept that literals cannot be symbolized, or find another resolution.
The Resolution Through Symbolic Conferral
The resolution emerges through recognizing that when (x) =(x)> x exists, it conveys that x =x> x. The symbol confers properties onto the referent—just as words convey meaning about reality. The existence of the symbol makes the self-relationship real through "mild anthropomorphism"—treating the literal as if it could relate to itself, even though by definition it cannot.
Grounding Examples
Consider equality and reference, which must be self-referential by their definitions:
For equality: x =eq> y <iff> x = y (where = is first-order logic equality) Therefore: eq =eq> eq (equality relates to itself through equality)
For reference: A[x]: ref =ref> x (ref refers to every referent) Therefore: ref =ref> ref (ref must refer to itself)
These aren't arbitrary examples but demonstrations of how certain fundamental concepts must be self-referential to fulfill their definitions. The pattern reveals how symbolizing a relationship places it in an objective role, following the abstract form rel =rel> obj.
The Two Beliefs of Symbolization
When we symbolize something, we assert two things:
x =x> x - The literal can relate to itself (the anthropomorphic fiction)
(x) =(x)> (x) - The symbol relates to itself (lifted symbolically)
These are necessary fictions that enable representation. Without them, symbolization cannot occur.
The Kantian Perspective
SRT doesn't model Kant's noumena—the thing-in-itself. That is inaccessible, outside our reference frame. Everything in a catalogue has already entered representation. We face a fundamental choice:
If literals are literals (noumenal): x !=x> x, they cannot be symbolized
If literals represent literals (phenomenal): x =x> x marks their symbolizability
Canonical vs Perspectival SRT
In canonical SRT, attempting to represent objective reality, x =x> x serves as a marker:
For literals where it holds: they can be symbolized
For literals where it doesn't: they're parts of objects, not independently symbolizable
In perspectival SRT, where everything is already representation, x =x> x becomes axiomatic. No perspective is objective, even when representing objectivity. Everything that can be referred to exists in representation—the representation of language at least.
The Deep Implication
Believing in symbolization is believing in the existence of an outside world—of things that are literal, objective. But paradoxically, the moment we symbolize them, we bring them into representation. The symbol(x) creates the substrate for identity, while x =x> x expresses that x can have one.
This reveals that identity isn't imposed on referents but emerges from the possibility of symbolization. The axiom of self-possession captures this: having a symbol means your self-relationship becomes constitutive of what you are.
The Virtual Relationships: Has and Is
Identity enables two virtual relationships that participate in dichotomies.
The "Is" Relationship
The statement "x is its identity" translates to the canonical referring back to the entity:
text
x =|is> (x) := (x) =(x)> x
This captures first-person assertions like "I am Doug" which from third-person perspective become "Doug refers to someone." Both express the same underlying relationship where the identity refers to the entity through itself.
The "Has" Relationship
The statement "x has property p" translates to the identity referring to the entity through that property:
text
x =|has> p := (x) =(p)> x
This captures first-person assertions like "I have hair" which from third-person perspective become "Doug refers to someone with hair." The identity mediates possession through symbolic reference.
Both virtual relationships participate in their own dichotomies—is/am, has/belongs-to—but they themselves are not a dichotomy with each other.
Identity as Symbolic Proxy
The canonical symbol (x) serves three crucial roles in the semantic architecture.
First, it acts as a self-proxy, representing x's self-relationship (x,x). Second, it serves as a relation-proxy, mediating x's relationships with others through ((x),y). Third, it functions as a property-proxy, lifting x's properties to symbolic form through inheritance patterns like (x) -> (p).
The Complete Identity Equation
The full meaning of identity is captured in this self-referential equation:
text
(x) =(x)> x & ((x),x) == (x) & x =(x)> x
This equation establishes three facts. The canonical refers to x through itself. The canonical is the most specific relationship between itself and x. The entity possesses its identity as a property. Together, these create the self-referential loop that constitutes identity.
Example: A Dog with Fur
Consider a dog with the property of having fur. Beginning with the literal property:
srt
dog =fur> dog
dog =|has> id
Since the dog has identity, its canonical inherits from id:
text
(dog) -> id
The identity then generates the symbolic relationship:
srt
dog =fur> dog =|> (dog) -> (fur) =|> (dog) =(fur)> dog
Therefore we can express:
text
dog =|has> fur
Now consider the dog chasing a cat. The literal relationship:
srt
dog =chases> cat
Through identity, this generates multiple levels of inheritance:
srt
dog =chases> cat =|> (dog,cat) -> chases
dog =chases> cat =|> ((dog),cat) -> (chases)
dog =chases> cat =|> (dog) =(chases)> cat
The dog's identity becomes the symbolic subject that chases the cat, with the relationship lifted to symbolic form at multiple levels.
Identity and Reference Frames
Identity is always relative to a reference frame. Within frame F[@], the canonical symbol is bound to the frame through:
text
@ =@> (x)
This establishes that x has identity within the context of the frame, where @ (the referent associated with the frame) acts as the frame's representation. The identity (x) exists not in absolute terms but relative to the semantic context established by the frame. Different frames may yield different identities for the same referent, as the canonical symbol (x) inherits from and relates to the frame type @.
Identity and Representation
In the context of representation, identity enables the transformation from literals to symbols:
text
Literature(L): {dog, cat, fur}
Catalogue(L): {(dog), (cat), (fur)}
Each literal in the Literature gains identity through its canonical symbol in the Catalogue. These symbols then mediate all relationships in the symbolic realm of representation.
The Semantic Achievement
Identity as generator reveals a profound truth: to have identity is not merely to be named but to possess a symbolic proxy through which all one's relationships can be expressed. The identity (x) doesn't describe x's properties and relationships—it generates the entire symbolic apparatus through which x participates in meaning.
Formal Properties
Uniqueness: Each entity has at most one identity, corresponding to one canonical symbol.
Completeness: If x has identity, all its relationships lift to symbolic form through the generator theorems.
Coherence: The lifted symbolic relationships preserve the structure of literal relationships through inheritance patterns.
Self-Reference: Identity creates genuine self-reference without paradox through the equation ((x),x) == (x).
Conclusion
Identity in SRT is the mechanism by which entities enter the symbolic realm. Through the generator pattern, every literal relationship becomes a symbolic one, every property becomes a possession, and every reference becomes mediated through identity. This is not merely naming—it is the creation of a complete symbolic proxy that enables participation in representation, meaning, and ultimately, consciousness itself.

x =x> x - The literal can relate to itself (the anthropomorphic fiction)
(x) =(x)> (x) - The symbol relates to itself (lifted symbolically)
These are necessary fictions that enable representation. Without them, symbolization cannot occur.
The Kantian Perspective
SRT doesn't model Kant's noumena—the thing-in-itself. That is inaccessible, outside our reference frame. Everything in a catalogue has already entered representation. We face a fundamental choice:
If literals are literals (noumenal): x !=x> x, they cannot be symbolized
If literals represent literals (phenomenal): x =x> x marks their symbolizability
Canonical vs Perspectival SRT
In canonical SRT, attempting to represent objective reality, x =x> x serves as a marker:
For literals where it holds: they can be symbolized
For literals where it doesn't: they're parts of objects, not independently symbolizable
In perspectival SRT, where everything is already representation, x =x> x becomes axiomatic. No perspective is objective, even when representing objectivity. Everything that can be referred to exists in representation—the representation of language at least.
The Deep Implication
Believing in symbolization is believing in the existence of an outside world—of things that are literal, objective. But paradoxically, the moment we symbolize them, we bring them into representation. The symbol(x) creates the substrate for identity, while x =x> x expresses that x can have one.
This reveals that identity isn't imposed on referents but emerges from the possibility of symbolization. The axiom of self-possession captures this: having a symbol means your self-relationship becomes constitutive of what you are.
The Virtual Relationships: Has and Is
Identity enables two virtual relationships that participate in dichotomies.
The "Is" Relationship
The statement "x is its identity" translates to the canonical referring back to the entity:
text
x =|is> (x) := (x) =(x)> x
This captures first-person assertions like "I am Doug" which from third-person perspective become "Doug refers to someone." Both express the same underlying relationship where the identity refers to the entity through itself.
The "Has" Relationship
The statement "x has property p" translates to the identity referring to the entity through that property:
text
x =|has> p := (x) =(p)> x
This captures first-person assertions like "I have hair" which from third-person perspective become "Doug refers to someone with hair." The identity mediates possession through symbolic reference.
Both virtual relationships participate in their own dichotomies—is/am, has/belongs-to—but they themselves are not a dichotomy with each other.
Identity as Symbolic Proxy
The canonical symbol (x) serves three crucial roles in the semantic architecture.
First, it acts as a self-proxy, representing x's self-relationship (x,x). Second, it serves as a relation-proxy, mediating x's relationships with others through ((x),y). Third, it functions as a property-proxy, lifting x's properties to symbolic form through inheritance patterns like (x) -> (p).
The Complete Identity Equation
The full meaning of identity is captured in this self-referential equation:
text
(x) =(x)> x & ((x),x) == (x) & x =(x)> x
This equation establishes three facts. The canonical refers to x through itself. The canonical is the most specific relationship between itself and x. The entity possesses its identity as a property. Together, these create the self-referential loop that constitutes identity.
Example: A Dog with Fur
Consider a dog with the property of having fur. Beginning with the literal property:
srt
dog =fur> dog
dog =|has> id
Since the dog has identity, its canonical inherits from id:
text
(dog) -> id
The identity then generates the symbolic relationship:
srt
dog =fur> dog =|> (dog) -> (fur) =|> (dog) =(fur)> dog
Therefore we can express:
text
dog =|has> fur
Now consider the dog chasing a cat. The literal relationship:
srt
dog =chases> cat
Through identity, this generates multiple levels of inheritance:
srt
dog =chases> cat =|> (dog,cat) -> chases
dog =chases> cat =|> ((dog),cat) -> (chases)
dog =chases> cat =|> (dog) =(chases)> cat
The dog's identity becomes the symbolic subject that chases the cat, with the relationship lifted to symbolic form at multiple levels.
Identity and Reference Frames
Identity is always relative to a reference frame. Within frame F[@], the canonical symbol is bound to the frame through:
text
@ =@> (x)
This establishes that x has identity within the context of the frame, where @ (the referent associated with the frame) acts as the frame's representation. The identity (x) exists not in absolute terms but relative to the semantic context established by the frame. Different frames may yield different identities for the same referent, as the canonical symbol (x) inherits from and relates to the frame type @.
Identity and Representation
In the context of representation, identity enables the transformation from literals to symbols:
text
Literature(L): {dog, cat, fur}
Catalogue(L): {(dog), (cat), (fur)}
Each literal in the Literature gains identity through its canonical symbol in the Catalogue. These symbols then mediate all relationships in the symbolic realm of representation.
The Semantic Achievement
Identity as generator reveals a profound truth: to have identity is not merely to be named but to possess a symbolic proxy through which all one's relationships can be expressed. The identity (x) doesn't describe x's properties and relationships—it generates the entire symbolic apparatus through which x participates in meaning.
Formal Properties
Uniqueness: Each entity has at most one identity, corresponding to one canonical symbol.
Completeness: If x has identity, all its relationships lift to symbolic form through the generator theorems.
Coherence: The lifted symbolic relationships preserve the structure of literal relationships through inheritance patterns.
Self-Reference: Identity creates genuine self-reference without paradox through the equation ((x),x) == (x).
Conclusion
Identity in SRT is the mechanism by which entities enter the symbolic realm. Through the generator pattern, every literal relationship becomes a symbolic one, every property becomes a possession, and every reference becomes mediated through identity. This is not merely naming—it is the creation of a complete symbolic proxy that enables participation in representation, meaning, and ultimately, consciousness itself.
The Semantics of Identity ⁅2⁆ v6
The Semantics of Identity ⁅2⁆ at version 6
The Semantics of Identity
The Identity as Symbolic Generator
Identity in SRT is not merely a label or property, it is a symbolic generator that transforms all of an entity's relationships into symbolic form. When we say something has identity, we mean it possesses a canonical symbol that serves as a proxy for all its relationships, both to itself and to others.
Formal Definition
An entity x has identity when its canonical symbol refers back to it and inherits from the concept of identity:
text
x =|has> id := x =(x)> x & (x) -> id
This establishes two requirements. First, the canonical symbol must refer to the entity through itself. Second, the canonical must inherit from identity as a type.
The Fundamental Theorem of Semantic Reference Theory
The entire theory rests on one principle that defines how reference preserves semantic structure:
srt
(x,y) -> t =|> ((x,y)) -> (t)
When a relationship inherits from a type, its symbol inherits from the symbol of that type. This preservation of inheritance through symbolism is the fundamental theorem (or perhaps axiom) of semantic reference theory.
When x equals y, relationships become properties:
srt
(x,x) -> p =|> ((x,x)) -> (p)
Symbol Properties and Their Consequences
The distribution theorem states that the symbol of a relationship equals the relationship between symbols:
text
((x,y)) == ((x),(y))
For self-reference, symbols exhibit complete self-identity:
text
((x),(x)) == (x)
Combining these theorems yields the paired lifting principles:
srt
x =t> y =|> (x) =(t)> (y)
x =p> x =|> (x) =(p)> (x)
The Constitution of Identity Through Symbolism
The profound consequence emerges when a symbol inherits from a property:
text
(x) -> (p)
Combined with identity (where the symbol refers to its referent through itself):
text
(x) =(x)> x
We derive the constitutive principle:
srt
(x) =(x)> x & (x) -> (p) =|> (x) =(p)> x
From the reader's perspective, (x) =(x)> x expresses something like "the word we use for x represents x specifically." When that word inherits from a property, it constitutes x having that property through symbolic expression.
Why This Is Fundamental
This theorem (that inheritance is preserved through symbolism) emerges from a unique form of necessity, similar to how Gödel's sentence G, once understood to express consistency, compels belief even as an unprovable statement requiring axiomatization.
We've worked to express the semantics of symbolism and the semantics of inheritance between relationships in SRT. Now we must ask: since symbols are relationships themselves, how is inheritance expressed between symbols for those relationships?
We are compelled by the semantics of reference (which is the semantics of symbolism) to believe:
srt
(x,y) -> t =|> ((x,y)) -> (t)
If we think we've captured symbolism correctly, and we believe symbols are relationships, then the symbolic structure of inheritance must be preserved under symbolization. Not because we decree it, but because the theory must be able to symbolize its own structures accurately.
Deriving the Symbol Properties
The Distribution Property
How do we conclude ((x,y)) == ((x),(y))?
We ask: have we captured the most specific relationship symbolically? If yes, then the symbol for the most specific relationship between x and y should be the most specific relationship between the symbols for x and y. The symbol distributes over the relationship because that's what it means to symbolize relationships accurately.
The Self-Collapse Property
How do we conclude ((x),(x)) == (x)?
This requires understanding representation. It's a theorem that:
srt
(x,y) =represents> x & (x,y) =represents> y
Therefore:
srt
(x,x) =represents> x
Now consider: (x,x) represents x. Can (x,x) be x? Only if x is symbolic.
But look at ((x,x)). Once we accept it means ((x),(x)), we know that ((x),(x)) represents-representing x. How do we represent representing x? Through ((x)).
What is a representation of a representation of x? For any such representation, it should be the canonical representation of x: (x).
Therefore:
text
((x),(x)) == (x)
The Axioms of Identity
From these derivations, we can state the axioms that constitute identity in SRT:
Axiom 1: The Axiom of Semantic Reference
srt
(x,y) -> t =|> ((x,y)) -> (t)
Inheritance is preserved through symbolization. This defines what it means for symbols to accurately represent relationships.
Axiom 2: The Axiom of Semantic Specification
text
((x,y)) == ((x),(y))
The symbol of a relationship equals the relationship between symbols. Symbolization distributes over relational structure, specifying relationships through their component symbols.
Axiom 3: The Axiom of Specific Representation
text
((x),(x)) == (x)
A symbol's relationship to itself is itself. This captures the complete self-identity that defines symbols as specific representations.
Axiom 4: The Axiom of Self-Possession
srt
x =|has> (x) =|> (x,x) == x
Having a canonical symbol means that the most specific self-relationship is the referent itself. When (x) exists, this expresses genuine self-possession. When (x) doesn't exist, the implication is vacuously true.
The Narrative of Symbolization and the Kantian Noumenon
The Problem of Literal Symbolization
From our derivations, we know that when x =p> x, then (x) -> (p) and therefore (x) =(p)> x. This would suggest that for the self-relationship x =x> x, we should get (x) =(x)> x. But this creates a paradox: literals by definition cannot be relational, yet symbolization seems to require x =x> x.
The Semantic Reference Dilemma
The axiom of semantic reference states (x,y) -> t =|> ((x,y)) -> (t). But what happens when (x,y) == t? We need to either restrict the axiom to cases where they differ, accept that literals cannot be symbolized, or find another resolution.
The Resolution Through Symbolic Conferral
The resolution emerges through recognizing that when (x) =(x)> x exists, it conveys that x =x> x. The symbol confers properties onto the referent (just as words convey meaning about reality). The existence of the symbol makes the self-relationship real through "mild anthropomorphism", treating the literal as if it could relate to itself, even though by definition it cannot.
Grounding Examples
Consider equality and reference, which must be self-referential by their definitions:
For equality: x =eq> y <iff> x = y (where = is first-order logic equality) Therefore: eq =eq> eq (equality relates to itself through equality)
For reference: A[x]: ref =ref> x (ref refers to every referent) Therefore: ref =ref> ref (ref must refer to itself)
These aren't arbitrary examples but demonstrations of how certain fundamental concepts must be self-referential to fulfill their definitions. The pattern reveals how symbolizing a relationship places it in an objective role, following the abstract form rel =rel> obj.
